title: Superpolynomial lower bounds for unrestricted Frege proofs
formal:
Is ordinary Frege not polynomially bounded? For the fixed calculus and complete binary encoding below, determine whether
\[\forall C,k\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \exists\varphi\;\bigl(\operatorname{Taut}(\varphi)\land\forall\pi\,[\operatorname{FProof}(\pi,\varphi)\Rightarrow |\pi|>C(|\varphi|+2)^k]\bigr).\]
Here \(\varphi\) ranges over finite propositional formulas, and \(\pi\) over finite binary strings. Equivalently, for every fixed polynomial bound, some tautology has minimum Frege proof size \(s_{\mathrm F}(\varphi)\) exceeding that bound in its own encoded length. Neither a polynomial-time construction of hard tautologies nor any algorithm for finding their shortest proofs is required. The depth and length of intermediate formulas and the reuse of previous lines are unrestricted.
definitions:
Ordinary propositional formulas are finite ordered syntax trees generated by variables \(x_i\), where \(i\in\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), unary negation \(\neg A\), and binary material implication \(A\to B\). A Boolean assignment gives every variable a value in \(\{0,1\}\); negation reverses it, and implication is false exactly when its antecedent is true and its consequent false. The predicate \(\operatorname{Taut}(\varphi)\) means that \(\varphi\) evaluates to true under every assignment to its variables. Formulas are fully written trees: repeated occurrences of a subformula are counted separately.

Fix exactly three axiom schemes:
\[A\to(B\to A),\qquad (A\to(B\to C))\to((A\to B)\to(A\to C)),\qquad (\neg B\to\neg A)\to(A\to B).\]
Each instance consistently replaces the metavariables \(A,B,C\) by arbitrary formulas. The only inference rule is modus ponens: from earlier lines \(A\) and \(A\to B\), infer \(B\). A proof is a nonempty finite sequence of axiom instances and such inferences, with its last formula the conclusion. There are no hypotheses, no extension axioms naming other formulas, and no separate rule substituting into a previously derived line. Variables absent from the final formula may appear in ordinary intermediate formulas. Earlier lines may be reused arbitrarily often, so the dependency graph need not be a tree. There is no cap on line size, logical depth, dependency-path length or number of lines.

Use the following explicit prefix encoding. For an integer \(t\ge0\), let \(b(t)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\), using concatenation. The formula \(x_i\) is encoded by tag 00 followed by \(E(i)\); a negation by tag 01 followed by the child formula; an implication by tag 10 followed by the antecedent and consequent formulas in order. Formula tag 11 is invalid. A proof of \(m\ge1\) lines starts with \(E(m)\). Each line then has a two-bit justification tag followed by its complete formula encoding. Tags 00, 01 and 10 identify the first, second and third axiom schemes, respectively; the written formula must be a syntactic instance of the indicated scheme. Tag 11 denotes modus ponens and is followed, after the formula, by \(E(a)E(b)\). On line \(j\), require \(1\le a,b<j\), line \(a\) to be some \(A\), and line \(b\) to be exactly \(A\to B\), where the current line is \(B\). Malformed strings are not proofs. This makes \(\operatorname{FProof}(\pi,\varphi)\) a specific syntactic validity predicate with final formula \(\varphi\), rather than a claim that unspecified inference rules are sound.

The lengths \(|\varphi|\) and \(|\pi|\) are their entire binary encoding lengths. Every connective, variable index, repeated subformula, line count and inference reference is included. A huge formula is not a constant-cost proof line; proof-size bounds are measured against the full conclusion length, not just its number of distinct variables. This finite Hilbert calculus is sound and complete for classical propositional tautologies. Therefore every tautology has some finite proof, and \(s_{\mathrm F}(\varphi)\) is the minimum bit length among its valid proof strings. Standard finite Frege presentations are polynomially equivalent, so this explicit convention fixes the meaning without changing polynomial boundedness. Restricting the coefficients and exponents of candidate polynomial bounds to positive integers also does not change the question.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. For an affirmative answer, prove that for every pair \(C,k\ge1\) there exists a genuine tautology for which every valid proof exceeds the specified size; an efficiently generated hard family is welcome but is not required. A negative answer must establish one fixed pair \(C,k\ge1\) such that every tautology has some valid Frege proof of size at most \(C(|\varphi|+2)^k\). It need not supply a polynomial-time proof-search algorithm. All formula semantics, syntactic verification and size claims must match the given model and be justified in Lean. A fixed-degree lower bound, an independent cap on line size or depth, a bound for a subsystem, or hardness of finding proofs does not answer the full question. The numerical 1/100 convention does not replace this binary asymptotic comparison.
why: This asks whether a standard, robust language of propositional deduction must sometimes use certificates larger than every polynomial in the statement proved. It is a central unresolved lower-bound question for formal reasoning, beyond the restricted proof systems for which strong size lower bounds are known. It concerns the size of the best possible proof, independently of the resources used to discover it.

importance.reason: A central unresolved step in the Cook–Reckhow program, beyond the systems for which current general lower-bound methods succeed.

progress.text: Cook and Reckhow relate existence of polynomially bounded proof systems to NP = coNP and prove robustness of standard Frege presentations.
Buss publishes polynomial-size Frege proofs of the pigeonhole principle, whose usual encoding is exponentially hard for resolution.
Wigderson retains the unrestricted lower-bound problem as Open Problem 6.10 in the final author draft, printed page 66.
Davis and Robere state quasipolynomial \(\operatorname{Res}(\log)\) refutations of assertions of short bounded-depth Frege proofs with a polynomial line-size cap.
De Rezende, Engström, Ghannane and Risse report average-case superpolynomial length bounds for tree-like Frege and semantic extensions with a separate bounded line-size requirement.
Alekseev publishes the rational algebraic extension-rule bit-size lower bound, explicitly distinguishing its input from the propositional CNF case needed for a Frege lower bound.
ECCC TR26-166 reiterates the unrestricted Frege frontier while reporting a quasipolynomial upper simulation bound for restricted partially commutative formula IPS.

status_note: Open in Wigderson’s checked 6 August 2019 draft and reiterated in the September 2026 primary literature. Bounded checks through 15 September 2026 identified no unconditional superpolynomial bit-size lower bound for unrestricted Frege and no universal polynomial upper bound. The April tree-like result has a separate line cap, the refutation-principle result has bounded-depth/line parameters and quasipolynomial overhead, and the June algebraic theorem does not transfer its hard instance to the required propositional setting. New proofs were not independently verified.

context_blocks.text: Frege systems formalize ordinary propositional deduction with finitely many rule patterns. A proof can derive intermediate lemmas, combine them and cite them again. Checking a proposed step is a syntactic task with polynomial cost in its written size. The question asks whether some short true statements inevitably require much larger certificates in this particular language, even when no restrictions are placed on intermediate formulas.

The distinction between statement length and variable count matters. A formula on \(n\) variables can itself have exponential length in \(n\), so an exponential bound expressed only in the variable count need not be large compared with the actual input. This card compares total proof bits directly with \(|\varphi|\). It also distinguishes the number of proof lines from their combined size: a single enormous intermediate assertion is fully charged.

Cook and Reckhow show that some polynomially bounded propositional proof system exists if and only if \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). Thus \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\) would imply a positive answer here, and polynomial boundedness of Frege would imply \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). A lower bound for this one fixed proof language does not by itself establish that no other proof language is polynomially bounded. The card asks for an unconditional answer and does not assume a complexity-class separation.

Short proofs and efficient proof discovery are separate resources. The positive statement quantifies over all candidate polynomial size bounds, then permits a different hard tautology for each bound. It does not impose a construction algorithm for those tautologies. Conversely, a universal polynomial upper bound would assert that short certificates exist, without by itself giving a polynomial-time algorithm that finds them.

The propositional pigeonhole principle asserts that \(n+1\) pigeons cannot be injected into \(n\) holes. Its familiar CNF encoding requires exponential-size resolution refutations, while Buss proved polynomial-size Frege proofs in 1987. This is a concrete separation between a weaker clause-based system and Frege. It also explains why a hard family for one proof system cannot automatically be treated as hard for every stronger system. The original author abstract and theorem statements were checked, together with Wigderson's textbook account.

Wigderson states the unrestricted question as Open Problem 6.10 in the author draft of 6 August 2019, on printed page 66, following the pigeonhole upper bound in Theorem 6.9. The older cached March 2018 draft has different pagination; the 2019 file was checked separately in this review. Arbitrary intermediate formulas are part of this problem even when the final tautology is shallow. A theorem limiting only bounded-depth proofs does not cover deductions using deeper formulas.

De Rezende, Engström, Ghannane and Risse's April 2026 preprint states average-case superpolynomial refutation-length bounds for tree-like semantic Frege with a separate line-size cap. Corollary 1.6 considers \(n^{2-\varepsilon}\le s(n)\le2^{n^{1-\varepsilon}}\), with source-prescribed fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), and an explicit family of CNFs of size at most \(s(n)^{1+\varepsilon}\); a uniformly sampled member is hard with probability tending to one for tree-like proofs whose individual lines have size at most \(s(n)\). The conclusion concerns that capped system and the stated distribution, not every member or every unrestricted Frege proof. The arXiv submission is dated 30 April; the downloaded typescript is headed 1 May.

The line cap is material. Without a separate line-size cap, ordinary tree-like Frege polynomially simulates general Frege. The cited paper explains that the known conversion increases individual formula sizes, so it does not preserve the capped model used by its lower bound. In the stronger semantic setting, allowing a line large enough to represent the entire inconsistent input even permits an immediate semantic contradiction. None of this supplies a lower bound for unrestricted syntactic Frege.

Davis and Robere's 10 April 2026 report concerns proofs of statements about proof lengths. Its refutation-principle formula asserts that a specified pigeonhole CNF has a depth-\(d\) Frege refutation with a prescribed number of lines, each of polynomially bounded size. Theorem 1.3 gives refutations of those assertions in \(\operatorname{Res}(\log)\), where lines are DNFs with logarithmically bounded conjunction width. The bound is quasipolynomial in the length of the encoded refutation-principle assertion; it is not a polynomial upper bound in the original pigeonhole parameter. The depth and line-size restrictions on the asserted proofs remain essential.

Alekseev's journal paper, published 21 June 2026 after a CCC 2021 precursor, proves an exponential bit-size lower bound over \(\mathbb Q\) for Polynomial Calculus with extension and square-root rules. Its Binary Value Principle instance consists of \(1+\sum_{i=1}^{n}2^{i-1}x_i=0\) and \(x_i^2-x_i=0\). The paper explicitly notes that this algebraic input is not the relevant polynomial-size propositional CNF translation, so the theorem does not yield Frege or EF lower bounds. This is a limit on transferring that specific lower bound, not a claim that no Boolean encoding of the arithmetic condition can exist.

Extended Frege additionally permits variables naming intermediate formulas. A lower bound for EF would imply one for Frege, while a Frege lower bound need not persist in the presence of those definitions. Separating Frege from EF is also a different question: Frege could have hard tautologies that are equally hard for EF. The present target requires only failure of a universal polynomial bound for Frege itself.

The September 2026 report on partially commutative Ideal Proof Systems again records that unrestricted Frege has no known superpolynomial lower bound. Its own theorem is an upper bound: a quasipolynomial Frege simulation of a restricted algebraic formula system over \(\mathrm{GF}(2)\). This fresh source supplies dated context, not a proof of the present conjecture. The model restrictions and complete new proof have not been independently validated beyond the source-scope review.

sentences: Ordinary Frege is a fixed finite calculus for propositional reasoning that allows arbitrary intermediate formulas and unrestricted reuse of earlier deductions.
The question asks whether every proposed polynomial bound fails to cover the shortest Frege proofs of some genuine tautologies.
Both the conclusion and the entire proof are measured by explicit binary encodings, including repeated formulas and inference references.
Known lower bounds with depth, tree or line-size restrictions and recent algebraic lower bounds do not settle the unrestricted comparison.
A complete Lean proof must establish failure of every universal polynomial bound or prove one bound for all tautologies, without an additional proof-search or hard-family construction requirement.
